doc.title: Ken Peplowski interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Opening and the working musician's life
title: Welcome at Aspen and the hard reality of travel
summary: Rowe welcomes Peplowski; he says the glamour hides hard touring, and Warren Vache's line that musicians are paid for the traveling.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: We are filming today in Aspen, Colorado, and it’s a great pleasure for me to welcome Ken Peplowski, clarinetist and tenor saxophonist.
This kind of seems like heaven here to me. I mean you get invited to play jazz with some great musicians in this beautiful surrounding. How did you manage that?
How did I manage it? I picked up the phone.

Well I mean there’s obvious plusses and minuses to this. It sounds like a great, glamorous life to people that don’t do it. But it’s not as easy as it sounds. I mean this is a luxury to be in a place for even four or five days like this, and not have to travel a lot. When I do my own tours, in fact I have one coming up in Spain, and it’s going to be all one-nighters, sometimes playing with local rhythm sections, which you’re never sure about, and it’s a lot of hard traveling and then you have to show up to the job and play as if you’re incredibly happy to be there playing with this fine band. Because the audience doesn’t know about that stuff, nor should they.
Right. If you were to tell them that boy it sure was hard getting here today, what’s the difference to them?

Yeah. And there’s a friend of mine, Warren Vache, who said it’s not the traveling — we don’t get paid for the music, we get paid for the traveling. And that’s really what it’s all about because the music makes it worth while, as cliché as that sounds, there’s no other reason why we would do something like this.
